chapter_theme: The women take the Jain vow: three sights of fallen wealth, cloth and youth turn Sunandai and Civakan to renunciation, the matrons go in palanquins to Pammai's nunnery, are washed, bound, stripped, shorn and filled with virtue while the king bows at their feet, and he and Nandattan protest and are answered.

cast.role: the unnamed voice of the three sights of 2624-2626, probably the nun-teacher; nothing in the verses names the speaker
the hero, now king, left behind by the women who renounce
Kantukkatan's wife, who reared Civakan and is Nandattan's mother; she takes the vow
the two matrons who leave in palanquins to renounce (probably Vijayai and Sunandai; the verse names neither)
the women who go to Pammai's nunnery and take the vow
the head nun, whose nunnery the women reach and who teaches and answers
the matron who has taken the vow, silent before the king in 2642 and the lady ascetic of 2648
a thousand maidens who catch the shorn hair on gold trays
Civakan's army that carries flowers behind him
the women ascetics of the nunnery
the great queens, whom the nuns send to speak kindly to Civakan
Civakan's younger brother and Sunandai's son

2624.reading: The sermon points to a woman who once drank boiled milk from a golden bowl and now, worn by hunger and cut off from her fortune by cruel deeds, stands bent like a creeper with a wide bowl held out, crying 'alms'; seeing her, the rich are told not to trust their wealth and to think on good dharma.
2624.nuance: The fall is put to வெவ்வினை (cruel deeds), so the picture is an instance of karma ripening and not mere chance. The same closing refrain, நல்லறமே நினைமின் கண்டீர், ends 2625 and 2626, so the three verses are three sights under one refrain: food, cloth, youth. The verse does not name the speaker or the hearers; the refrain addresses the rich (செல்வ).

claims.claim: wealth is no ground for trust, since cruel deeds can bring one fed from gold to beg, so one should turn the mind to good dharma

2625.reading: A second sight: a woman once in bright silk, now in a small torn cloth that she wears half and holds half, who weeps day by day 'alas, my deeds'; the rich are told not to cling to wealth and to think on good dharma.
2625.nuance: She herself cries அந்தோ வினையே ('alas, my deeds'), so the sermon takes karma from the sufferer's own mouth. The simile in line 3 (அண்ணாந்த தடகுரீஇ) is hard to construe and is left out of the reading.

claims.claim: the fall from silk to rags is the working of one's own deeds, so wealth gives nothing to hold

2626.reading: A third sight: a youth in a jasmine garland, spear in hand, whom women gazed at as at Kama, comes to lean on a staff, his understanding thrust out by the phlegm that rattles in his throat, and he stands drooling like melted ghee: youth does not last.
2626.nuance: The verse turns on a single person shown before and after, so the loss is felt as one life's, not as a general remark; the refrain here reads நிலையாதே காண் (it does not stay) in place of the refrain of 2624-2625.

claims.claim: youth and beauty do not last, for age drives out understanding and leaves the body a ruin

2627.reading: Sunandai answers that the lady has seen it herself, and whether it be so or not she too has joined in and will renounce; at that Civakan stands melted like a hill of butter over a bright fire, with no hold on himself and unmindful of his body.
2627.nuance: That இறைவி means the nun who has just told the three sights, and that the one who melts in line 4 is Civakan, are inferred from this verse alone; the speaker of யானும் ஒன்றினன் துறப்பல் could also be read as Civakan.
2627.event: Sunandai declares that she too will renounce, and Civakan stands melted and unmindful of his body.

2628.reading: As if two bodies were going and leaving one life behind, the matrons go in palanquins to their noble renunciation and the noble one is left, and the eyes of the women stream like rain.
2628.nuance: ஆரியன் is taken as Civakan, the one the two matrons leave, and the matrons as Vijayai and Sunandai; the verse names neither. In line 2 the matrons are written அங் கௌவை மார்கடாம், read here as அங்கு ஔவைமார்.
2628.event: The two matrons go in palanquins to take the vow, leaving Civakan behind, while the women weep.

2629.reading: The city is told to be thrown into uproar like a sea struck by the wind, with weeping voices mingling and flowers torn off.
2629.nuance: Line 1 (நன்மயிற் பொறியின்மேற் போயா நாளினும்) and the words மன்னனி லாகுலம் in line 4 are hard to construe; the reading keeps only the simile and the weeping.

2630.reading: After weeping, she goes through the decked city among a thousand worshipful palanquins and comes to the nunnery of Pammai of unblemished fame.
2630.nuance: The singular அன்னவள் is left unnamed; whether she is one of the matrons or a queen is not said.
2630.event: A woman, followed by a thousand palanquins, goes to Pammai's nunnery.

2631.reading: As Pammai sits like a creeper among a throng of creeper-like women ascetics and tells the dharma, the long-eyed woman comes down, joins her hands in worship and begs the lady to take them all in and save them.
2631.nuance: The one who asks is not named, and எமை (us) shows she speaks for more than herself.
2631.event: A woman alights before Pammai, worships, and asks to be taken in with the others.

2632.reading: Pammai tells her that penance is as hard as a lotus in a fierce fire, but that a gift sown in good ground and watered with virtue (சீலநீர்) grows sweet on the earth, gives many kinds of fame and afterwards gives the pleasures of the garlanded gods.
2632.nuance: The reward named is fame and heaven, not release: the nun sets the gift of the householder below the rare penance she is about to grant, in the epic's own order of fruit. The speaker is known only by the closing என்றாள் and the situation.
2632.event: Pammai tells the woman the reward of a gift sown with virtue, and that penance is harder.

claims.claim: a gift sown in good ground and watered with virtue brings fame in this world and the pleasures of the gods after it, while true penance is harder

2633.reading: Having heard the dharma again, they ask the lady to grant them renunciation quickly; then they raise a pure hall, hang fragrant garlands, spread a canopy like the sky, and set a seat, incense and bright lamps.
2633.event: The women ask for renunciation and prepare the hall of ordination.

2634.reading: They wash her small feet with milk and, by the rule, bind fine white cloth woven of thread round her breasts, as if blindfolding Death.
2634.nuance: The simile காலனைக் கண்புதைத்தாங்கு makes the binding a way of blinding Death; who binds and who is bound is not named.
2634.event: The women's feet are washed with milk and white cloth is bound on them by rule.

2635.reading: They scatter garlands and ornaments, wrap their breasts' broad court in soft cloth pale as moonlight, and so sow white thorns on the road by which Kama, lord of spring, would come.
2635.nuance: Line 3 (தானுரலாய்த் தடமுலை முற்றம் சூழ்ந்தரோ) is hard to construe; the reading follows its general sense.
2635.event: The women throw off garlands and ornaments and put on plain white cloth.

claims.claim: renunciation shuts the road by which desire comes

2636.reading: Facing east, the women sit on seats of fine blooms and let fall their hair like many peahens shedding feathers.
2636.event: The women sit facing east and shed their hair.

2637.reading: The matrons, their dark hair reddened by the jewelled comb, pluck it out themselves without a flinch, and enter renunciation pondering the settled meaning of the book the Lord spoke.
2637.nuance: Only பரமன் is said; that he is the Jina is the work's setting, not this verse's words. The women pull their own hair out, which the verse presents as done without flinching (பணிவிலர்).
2637.event: The matrons pluck out their own hair and take the vow.

claims.claim: renunciation is entered through reflection on the settled meaning of the scripture the Lord taught

2638.reading: A thousand maidens like golden creepers carry gold trays and catch the golden hair so that it does not touch the good ground, and the women who shed their old hair look like dancing peahens.
2638.event: A thousand maidens catch the women's hair on gold trays.

2639.reading: As if pouring jewels into gold pots, they fill the bone-body with virtues, spread and guard compassion over every living thing, and turn their thought to the nectar of the one who knows all.
2639.nuance: எற்புடம்பு names the body as bones, a frame to be filled with virtues where the preceding verses took ornaments off it. Line 2 prints பெண்ணிலாக் (womanless), which sits oddly with எண்ணிலாக் (countless); the reading keeps the plain sense of a full body of virtues.
2639.event: The new nuns fill themselves with virtues and compassion and look to the nectar of the all-knowing.

claims.claim: the ascetic guards every living being with compassion
the nectar of release is what the all-knowing one teaches

2640.reading: Neither glad at praise nor pitying scorn, having dug into the Anga books and packed their hearts with the rare meanings, they became the tilaka of the order, shining like a burning lamp.
2640.event: The new nuns study the Anga books and shine as the order's ornament.

claims.claim: the ascetic is unmoved by praise and by scorn
the ascetic's heart is stored with the meanings of the Anga scriptures

2641.reading: With elephants, chariots, horses and the sea-like army carrying flowers, the king himself bears a few blooms, goes and praises them richly, and touches his beautiful crown to the feet that are dyed red like cotton and lac.
2641.nuance: Whose feet they are is not said; the new nuns of 2636-2640 are the natural referent.
2641.event: Civakan and his army carry flowers to the new nuns, and he bows his crowned head at their feet.

2642.reading: The lord says he did harsh things before and asks that the lady stay a few days in the city so that he may see her with his own eyes; she gives the crowned king no word, standing like an image, and seeing it Pammai replies.
2642.nuance: That the lord is Civakan and that தேவி is a matron now ordained (not a queen of his house) are inferred from the sequence; the verse gives neither a name.
2642.event: Civakan asks the lady to stay a few days; she is silent and Pammai answers for her.

2643.reading: Pammai tells the king that he is no longer her lover and that she and the others are strangers to him; and the garlanded man, undone of his claim and himself, wrenches at his flower wreath and laments as his tears pour.
2643.nuance: Which side of the break lines 1-2 name (the lady's, or the nuns') is hard to fix; உரிமையுந் தானுமாதோ is read as the king losing both his right and himself.
2643.event: Pammai tells him he has no more claim on her, and Civakan weeps and laments.

claims.claim: one who has taken the vow is no longer a husband's own, and the order is a stranger to his claim

2644.reading: The nuns, moved by the Lords' dharma, say that though he is a stranger to them he is dear to the order, and tell the great queens to give the king gentle words, for he has done no wrong.
2644.nuance: The line-by-line sense of lines 1-2 is uncertain and the reading gives only its general turn.
2644.event: The nuns urge the great queens to speak kindly to Civakan.

2645.reading: Addressing him as the spear-bearer with the diamond-hill shoulders and the garland, they say they have asked what they wished; his heart cools and he speaks.
2645.nuance: Who the speakers are is taken from the preceding verse, which sends the nuns' message to the great queens.
2645.event: The queens tell Civakan they have asked what they wished, and he answers with a cool heart.

2646.reading: Crying that the lady may go but that the rest who joined are nothing to him, he cries to Sunandai that she has given him a burning grief and is no mother, and calls her cruel again and again, like a lion in distress crying before its mother.
2646.nuance: The speaker is taken as Nandattan, Sunandai's son, because the simile has a lion crying before its mother and 2648 answers Nandattan; Civakan, her foster son, is possible.
2646.event: He rebukes Sunandai for leaving, calling her no mother.

2647.reading: A woman answers that what has gone is gone: if, now that this lady has renounced today, she herself sat on in the king's realm, the blame would never leave her; and with these words to cool the golden-hill-like hero she bids him go in to the palace.
2647.nuance: Whether இவள் is the speaker herself or the lady who has renounced, and who the speaker is, cannot be fixed from this verse.
2647.event: She consoles him and asks him to return to the palace.

2648.reading: The lady ascetic tells Nandattan, whose garland tore the bosoms of ball-playing women, that he need not be hurt and angry, for they have not given him up; and the strong-shouldered man opens like a wish-tree in bloom.
2648.nuance: நங்கையார் அடிகள் is read as the matron who has taken the vow, Nandattan's mother Sunandai; the verse does not name her.
2648.event: The lady ascetic comforts Nandattan that she has not forsaken him.

links.note: Naladiyar 1 shows men who ate six-flavoured meals served by a willing wife and then beg gruel here and there; 2624 shows a woman who drank boiled milk from a golden bowl and now holds out a wide bowl for alms.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar's quatrain draws the rule that wealth cannot be counted on, and the Cintamani turns the same beggar's fall into a sight the preacher points to while urging the hearers to turn to dharma.

gains.a: the sermon verse gets an old, general proof (those who ate richly and then beg) behind its single sight, so the woman reads as a type and not a pity
gains.b: the quatrain gets a woman, her hunger and the posture of begging bent like a creeper, which it lacks as an anonymous list of eaters, and the sermon's turn from the picture to dharma

links.note: The woman of 2624 would give anything for boiled milk in a golden bowl; in 354 the good women offer milk-nectar in a gold vessel to Vijayai in the ascetic's hermitage, and she will not even look at it.
links.teaches: The milk in the gold vessel is the same thing wanted by one and refused by the other, so the epic puts the beggar's lack and the nun's refusal on one object to show what renunciation means as a choice.

links.note: In 303 the woman who once went into sky-touching palaces like a heavenly maiden is left alone in a forest of white skulls and is said to be shown so that hearers may see sin; 2625 offers another woman in a half-covered rag as the same lesson.
links.teaches: What the epic first set before the eye as Vijayai's own fall is later handed on as a spoken example, so the story and the sermon the story ends in draw on one fund of images.

links.note: Naladiyar 13 shows those whose speech fails, who lean on a staff and lose their teeth, yet stay in the house with their eyes on desire; 2626 shows a youth in a garland and spear who comes to lean on a staff and drool.
links.teaches: The sermon shows the young man whose decline the Naladiyar describes only from its end, and so makes the same warning about desire outliving the body's strength.

gains.a: the epic's youth gets the Naladiyar's charge that the old man who lingers in the house is blind to the road to safety, which the sermon only implies
gains.b: the quatrain gets the garland-and-spear picture of the youth before, which it lacks, so its old man is someone who was once the Kama of women's eyes

links.note: The patikam says that while kings paid tribute and his sceptre ran, Civakan heard the dharma and was afraid of kingship like a snake; in 2627 Sunandai says she will renounce too and Civakan melts.
links.teaches: The turn the patikam gave in one line is shown here as it happens, in the answer of a mother and the dissolving of a king, not as a decision of his own.

links.note: 2628 has the matrons go in palanquins to their renunciation; Tirumanthiram 153 has the lord of the town mount for the last time a palanquin of the burning ground.
links.teaches: One kind of vehicle is shown going two ways: a rich woman's palanquin carries her to a life given up while still alive, and the lord's palanquin carries him to the burning ground whether he chooses or not.

gains.a: the epic palanquin gets the Tirumanthiram's irony that the ride of honour ends in the burning ground, so the matrons' ride reads as taking that last ride first and by choice
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's palanquin gets a counter-case in which the ride is boarded willingly before death, which its picture of the lord's last journey leaves out

links.note: Kural 47 puts the householder who lives the household life rightly first among all who strive; 2632 has the nun say that penance is hard and that a gift sown with virtue yields fame and then the pleasures of the gods.
links.teaches: The Jain nun grades the gift of the householder as a fruit of fame and heaven and keeps the harder penance above it, so the Kural's 'first among strivers' is put against a ladder of fruits.

gains.a: the nun's rule that gift watered with virtue gives fame and heaven gets a rival ranking that puts the householder at the head of all effort
gains.b: the couplet, which does not say what is striven for, gets one answer: for the Jain the striving is for fame and heaven by gift, or for more by penance

links.note: 2635 has the women fling off garlands and ornaments and sow thorns on Kama's road; Siddhar 19 asks when the singer shall leave silk clothes, gold ornaments, pretence and evil deeds and desire the Lord's feet.
links.teaches: Both strip off ornament, but one is done as a rite with no god in it and the other is a longing aimed at a god's feet.

gains.a: the epic stripping gets the Siddhar's aim, the Lord's feet, which the verse leaves blank, and shows that its rite aims only at closing Kama's road
gains.b: the Siddhar's longing gets a finished ritual, a fixed hall and day, where the song only asks 'when shall I'

links.note: In 350 Vijayai takes off the tilaka, earrings, neck ornaments and the pearls on her breasts when she is received into the hermitage; 2635 has the women scatter garlands and ornaments in a prepared hall.
links.teaches: What one forlorn queen did alone in a forest is done here as an ordered rite for many, so the epic shows renunciation first as a refuge and last as an institution.

links.note: Kural 280 says neither shaving nor long hair is needed if one gives up what the world condemns; 2637 has the matrons pluck out their own dark hair and enter renunciation pondering the settled meaning of the Lord's book.
links.teaches: The Jain rite of plucking the hair is joined to inward thought in the verse, which is the answer to the Kural's doubt whether the shorn head means anything without giving up.

gains.a: the plucking is given a test, whether it comes with giving up what is condemned, which the epic verse supplies only as pondering the scripture
gains.b: the couplet gets a rite that is neither shaving nor matting, hair plucked by one's own hand, which it does not consider

links.note: In 349 Vijayai takes off the gold garland and necklace while her musk-dressed hair grieves; in 2637 the matrons themselves pluck their dark hair without a flinch.
links.teaches: The grief of the hair in the forest is replaced by an act done without bowing, so the epic shows the same hair going first with sorrow and then with composure.

links.note: The patikam says that his younger brother, friends and richly adorned wives all renounce the things of sense; 2640 shows the new nuns studying the Anga books and shining as tilaka of the order.
links.teaches: What the patikam announced as a bare fact is shown here as a life of learning and equanimity.

links.note: After the last battle Civakan bows to the Jina and flings out gold before putting on his royal ornaments (2357); in 2641 he takes flowers and touches his crowned head to the nuns' feet.
links.teaches: The crown is lowered twice, first before the Jina in victory and last before the women who have given up, so the epic marks the end of his kingship by whom he bows to.

links.note: In 1915 Vijayai tells her son that his mother is Sunandai, always, and his father Kandukkatan; in 2646 Sunandai is called 'no mother' for leaving.
links.teaches: The mother whom the epic made the true one by love is accused of not being a mother when her vow takes her away from her son.

source_issues: 2624-2627 and 2642-2648 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
2628 line 2 prints அங் கௌவை மார்கடாஞ், read as அங்கு ஔவைமார்தாம் (the matrons).
2629 line 1 (நன்மயிற் பொறியின்மேற் போயா நாளினும்) and the words மன்னனி லாகுலம் in line 4 are hard to construe.
2635 line 3 (தானுரலாய்த் தடமுலை முற்றம் சூழ்ந்தரோ) is hard to construe.
2639 line 2 prints எற்புடம்பெண்ணிலாக்; பெண்ணிலாக் may be a misprint for எண்ணிலாக்.
2642-2648: who speaks and who is addressed is not named, and is inferred from the sequence.
